commenti.body: I think flashbacks *can* be a very nice tool for a filmmaker, and I think the use of flashbacks in The Godfather 2 is used very well. It is (arguably) among the top 5 films of all time, and any attempt at criticizing it will probably fall to deaf ears. That being said, I believe you have every right to like or dislike any aspect of any film, but to “dislike flashbacks in general” is to me a pretty weird statement. While I agree there are many films who use flashbacks poorly, *disliking* one of the most basic storytelling techniques *“in general”* is pretty far out there tbh.

I think OP needs to be more specific about what he dislikes.  All I can get from the post is that he dislikes flashbacks in general.  Which is certainly something…but regardless, I don’t even know if I would describe the young Vito parts of the Godfather as flashbacks in the traditional sense.  They aren’t used as a technique to tell the film’s main story; they are a fully independent storyline that is interwoven with Michael’s storyline.  Coppola was quoted on his intention to tell the story of both a father and son in one film.  Whether you think the two storylines properly inform each other in order to justify the split focus is up for debate, and people like Ebert have criticized it.

That’s a good point. When looking back at the film earlier, the juxtaposition of father and son was always my favorite part, but on my last rewatch I found it somewhat distracting. But unlike OP, the young Vito storyline is my favorite

I also like the young Vito storyline, though I do prefer Michael’s plot. I think you’ve misinterpreted my post; it’s not intended to be critique of the Godfather II. I love the Godfather II. I’m merely asking why the flashbacks in Part II work, which would then necessitate examples of movies where it doesn’t work, generating a discussion about the nature of flashbacks and how to properly implement them. Perhaps I was unnecessarily vague.

I once upon a time watched a cut of the film that was in chronological order. I think while it’s not a “vast” improvement, for me it improved the flow of the film(s). I agree with George Lucas’ assessment  and I paraphrase - “You have two great films here; lose one.” 

Thematically, I don’t think it entirely works cutting back and forth. The storylines do not naturally feed into one another. You lose nothing by excising the other. 

Both the prequel and sequel are expertly directed but as a viewer I feel like I’m getting jerked around once I’m invested in one timeline the rug is pulled out from under me and I have to reorient myself instead of remaining fully engaged.

My problem was merely with your statement regarding flashbacks in general, which I found quite odd. The use of flashbacks is a very common, and often effective, narrative tool used extensively both in films and literature. Naturally that will result in a lot of misuse, which I understand can have a negative effect on your view of them. Would you mind telling me why you generally dislike them? Did you see a lot of movies that uses flashbacks poorly, or would you generally dislike it even in films where it is executed well?
I used to have this on VHS, I believe it was called The Godfather Complete Epic and came with some extended/extra scenes.

>And what do you think the flashbacks accomplish, apart from the usual "it juxtaposes Vito's rise with Michael's fall".

  
50 years ago, when GODFATHER II was released, this wasn't considered "usual" -- it was a pretty daring storytelling choice.     I'm sure it has been imitated and homage-d since then.   But I think you would have trouble finding examples of successful films using flashbacks as rise/fall juxtaposition before that.

It was also a time that sequels were rarely done.    Today we are used to seeing FILM TITLE PART TWO, but when Coppola called his film "PART II" it was ballsy.    He was deliberately referencing Shakespeare (HENRY IV PART II, for instance), and announcing through the title it was an epic.

Yes, I think that’s what I watched once upon a time. I rented that not knowing it wasn’t the original version. I was just a kid after all, but after all these years I still prefer it. I wish there were a 4k of it.

>And what do you think the flashbacks accomplish, apart from the usual "it juxtaposes Vito's rise with Michael's fall".

I actually think that's the last things those flashbacks serve to show.

In tragedy - which is what The Godfather films are - the rise and fall of the character is not measure in materialistic aspects, its measured in the character's virtue, and so while the flashback Vito sequences show Vito rise in a materialistic sense, his too is a fall from virtue: from boy to family man to robber, murderer and mobster.

I should see the film again - something I must be frank I have little desire to do - to really decide with myself what if at all the flashback sequences DO achieve for me. I do think of them as well executed for what they are, and visually I love the way they look, so there's that.
It’s one of the reasons I think part 1 is a much better film.

The reason the flashbacks are included in GF2 is they are part of the Godfather novel. The novel is the first movie and the flashbacks of the second movie, going back and forth. So the story in the flashbacks already existed. Given the way the studio was on Coppola about the budget, it’s not a surprise that the flashbacks were not included in the first movie. But a Best Picture win gets you the opportunity to make a sequel and include the backstory. BTW the movies are very faithful to the novel with the exception of Kay. The novel ends describing Kay as accepting of her role as a mobster’s wife praying for the continued safety of Michael. We don’t get the “what did I get myself into” Kay we see in the first movie nor the defiant Kay we see in the sequel

It was definitely distracting at times and I was more involved with Michael's arc than Vito's. However, it also enhances the film into something much more memorable and challenging for better and worse so I'd rather have it than not. The parallel is awkward in the beginning but one does get used it. I think my only issue with the flashback is the actual content as it seemed to draw out a relatively simple story of Vito's origins. This disparity made it so Vito was a bit of a weigh to get to the better parts at times.
